extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of classic English literature; writers interested in rhetorical technique embedded in fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted implicit advice and evaluative observations about rhetoric, oratory, sensory imagery, and the author's writing process as presented within an 18th-century novel excerpt (Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of physical gesture in oratory (Trim's hat)
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical action (Trim dropping his hat) can embody and communicate a sentiment (mortality) more powerfully than words when executed properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dropping must suit the feeling: many ways of dropping a hat would produce no effect — flinging, throwing, casting, skimming, squirting, letting it slip, or doing it awkwardly would have failed. The exact manner and timing (pause before the word, the hat falling like a dead thing, the speaker's eye fixed on it) create the emotional impact. Performances of gesture should align with the sentiment they intend to represent; otherwise the effect is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrasting oratorical styles: ornate metaphorical vs plain natural
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasted modes of speech are presented: the father's learned, period-by-period, metaphor-and-allusion style (aimed at entertaining the fancy) versus Corporal Trim's plain, direct, unaffected speech (which goes straight to the heart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both styles have value: learned, allusive discourse delights fancy and displays wit; plain unadorned speech can reach the audience's heart more immediately. Choose style according to desired effect—picture-rich ornament for intellectual pleasure, simple natural speech for emotional directness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of visual imagery (the eye's commerce with the soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the senses, the eye has the quickest commerce with the soul and leaves an inexpressible impression on the fancy that words alone may fail to convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor vivid visual detail when you want to make a striking, immediate impression on readers; visual images often convey what words cannot fully express. Do not rely solely on abstract verbal description when a sensory (especially visual) depiction will be more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer's discipline and resistance (composition as warfare)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing for publication, first thoughts are often 'temptations' or captious; composition is presented as a struggle against prejudices and intrusive ideas—'a state of warfare'—in which resistance is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect slow progress and frequent self-correction; persistence, resistance to ill-formed initial impulses, and continued revision matter more than raw natural wit. Beware of letting inherited prejudices and commonplace nurse-clack dominate the work; actively resist them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing material to expand (avoid over-strict preplanning of book size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter ‘grows under our hands’; authors who promise a very small, tightly bounded volume (e.g., 'I'll write a duodecimo') often find the subject expanding and their early plans overtaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overconfine scope at the outset; be prepared for the work to develop and enlarge as you write. Rigid promises about final size can lead to frustration or useless early parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical and anecdotal example to bolster argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator/the father supports his arguments by citing classical anecdotes and examples (Vespasian, Galba, Socrates, Cornelius Gallus, etc.) as rhetorical ornaments and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical exempla can add weight and color to discourse, but may be used more for rhetorical effect than rigorous proof. Employ such examples to illustrate and enliven points, keeping in mind they can be superficial if not integrated critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel/overlapping narrative technique (kitchen/parlour dialogues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever something notable occurs in the parlour, a parallel conversation or commentary runs in the kitchen; the household's convention is to leave the door ajar so kitchen talk can 'carry on' alongside parlour events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simultaneous or overlapping scenes/dialogues to create depth, irony, and economy (one scene's labor is saved by another character's parallel response). Practically: introduce a mechanism (like an ajar door) to make overlapping discourse plausible and to enrich narrative texture.
